title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning with Secure Aggregation
summary: Undergraduate thesis: federated learning + secure aggregation + differential privacy, applied to wind farm SCADA telemetry. Small interactive diagrams build up to the real protocol visualiser, embedded live.

blocks.html:
Building a Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning System with Secure Aggregation

Undergraduate thesis: Bachelor of Engineering (Honours), University of Sydney, MINT Research Group. Supervised by Dr. Ali Shakiba.

Wind farms don't want to share their sensor data with each other, and honestly, fair enough: it's commercially sensitive. So this thesis builds a system that trains one shared model across several wind farms' data without any of that data ever leaving home, then goes a step further so the training process itself can't be watched either.

items: Wind farm operators each sit on rich turbine sensor data, but competitive and legal reasons keep it siloed. Individually too small to train much, collectively plenty.

The system: Federated Learning trains across farms without moving the data, Secure Aggregation stops the server from peeking at anyone's individual update, and Differential Privacy adds a formal guarantee on top if you want it.
Secure Aggregation turned out to be free: same accuracy as plain federated training. Differential Privacy is not free; it's a real and fairly steep cost, measured below.
Three small diagrams let you break each idea yourself before the actual protocol visualiser runs all three together on real data, at the end.

blocks.html:
Wind power is now a serious part of the global energy mix. Installed capacity passed 1,347 GW at the end of 2025, meeting over 11% of world electricity demand, and it's forecast to nearly double by 2030. Keeping that fleet running isn't cheap either: operations and maintenance account for roughly 20–25% of the levelised cost of wind energy, so better fault-detection models are a fairly direct lever on the cost of clean electricity.

The obstacle is data. Every wind farm operator collects rich SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) telemetry from its turbines, but that data almost never leaves the organisation. Competitive sensitivity and regulation like the GDPR make centralising it a non-starter, so you end up with a pile of data silos, each too small on its own to train a reliable model, but plenty in aggregate.

That gap is what this thesis actually set out to answer, and it comes down to two questions:

RQ1: how can Secure Multiparty Computation, and Secure Aggregation specifically, be integrated into a federated learning system to protect updates during aggregation?

RQ2: how much individual privacy do current secure aggregation protocols actually hold onto, once tested on a real regression task with wind turbine SCADA data, at a client count far smaller than the protocols were originally built for?

What follows trains one shared model across those silos without the raw data ever leaving any of them, using real turbine data from the public CARE benchmark (three wind farms), working through RQ1 and RQ2 in order. Each idea below gets its own small diagram first, and the full protocol visualiser, where they all run together on the real data, is waiting at the end.

Normally you'd centralise the data and train one model on all of it. Federated Learning flips that around: a shared model gets trained across distributed clients (here, wind farms) without any client's raw data ever leaving its own site.

Each round works the same way. The server broadcasts the current global model to the clients, each client trains it briefly on its own local data, and sends back only the resulting parameter adjustments, never the data itself.

Here's that written down, with the notation defined as we go: say there are K farms in total, labelled by an index k. Farm k holds nk of the training examples, out of n total across every farm combined. After training for one round (call it round t+1), farm k reports back its own updated weights, written wkt+1. The server's job is to combine everyone's report into one new shared model, wt+1, and it does that by giving each farm's report a say proportional to how much data it holds:

wt+1 ← Σk (nk / n) · wkt+1

In plain English, that just says: scale each farm's new numbers by its share of the total data, then add all those scaled numbers up. A farm holding ten times the data of its peers gets ten times the say in the result, which matters here since wind farms vary in fleet size by an order of magnitude. This scheme is called Federated Averaging, or FedAvg (McMahan et al., 2017), and it's the workhorse of the field. The diagram below shows exactly this arithmetic worked out for three clients, using a small 2-number vector in place of a full model.

blocks.caption: Click run round a few times and watch each farm's weight vector change and the arithmetic below update. Then take a farm offline and run it again: its row disappears from the sum, and the other two farms' shares grow to make up the difference.

blocks.label: wind farms in the CARE benchmark: the entire client population this trains across, and dozens of times smaller than FL was originally built for

blocks.html: FL was designed and proven at huge scale: Google's production deployment handles roughly 10 million daily active phones. Wind farm operators are the opposite: a handful of identifiable companies, each holding a large, high-quality dataset. That's the cross-silo regime, and it changes which problems actually matter, as the next section shows.

"The data never leaves the site" turns out to be an incomplete promise. The gradient update each client sends back still carries a lot of information about the data it came from: Geiping et al. showed you can reconstruct high-resolution training images from a single gradient vector, and all it takes is a standard honest-but-curious server, meaning one that follows the protocol correctly but reads every message it receives. Keeping data local isn't enough if the updates themselves leak it.

Secure Aggregation, from Bonawitz et al., closes that gap by masking each client's update before it reaches the server. Here's the notation: call any one client u, and its true update wu. Client u picks one private random number just for itself, bu (its self-mask), and separately agrees on a shared secret number with every other client v, written su,v, via Diffie–Hellman key exchange. The pair always agrees on matching opposite values, so client v holds sv,u = −su,v, the negative of client u's copy of that same shared secret. What client u actually sends is its true update plus its self-mask plus the sum of all those shared secrets:

ŷu = wu + bu + Σv≠u su,v

In plain terms: before sending anything, each client adds a random number to its own update (its private mask), plus one shared secret number per other client, agreed on in advance so no one else ever sees it. The result looks like meaningless noise on its own.

Now add up what every client sent. Each shared secret su,v shows up twice across the whole sum: once from client u's side (+su,v) and once from client v's side (−su,v, since sv,u = −su,v), so those cancel exactly. The self-masks bu are handled separately: rather than cancelling on their own, the server reconstructs and removes them using secret shares that surviving clients reveal in a final "unmask" step (the simplified widget below skips that extra step and just builds each client's whole mask to cancel directly). Either way, once every mask has been accounted for, the server is left holding exactly the true total:

Σu ŷu = Σu wu

In other words: add up everyone's disguised numbers, every secret cancels against its matching pair, and only the true total the server was allowed to see all along is left. Below, the same three farms mask their small weight vectors before sending them. See exactly what the server receives versus what each farm actually computed.

blocks.caption: Masking starts on: run a round and watch the "server receives" column turn into what looks like noise, yet it still sums correctly. Flip masking off to see the difference, then drop farms (click a name) until fewer than τ are left standing: the round aborts instead of revealing anything.

blocks.label: lose one farm and you're already at the abort boundary: at K=3, dropping a single client removes a third of the network, not a rounding error

blocks.html: SecAgg was designed and evaluated at K in the hundreds to millions, where losing a handful of clients barely registers. At K=3, that's a direct stress-test of RQ2: whether SecAgg's guarantees hold up gracefully at a client count this small, or whether something breaks.

SecAgg solves one problem, the server never sees any individual update, but it says nothing about what the aggregate itself reveals. That's what Differential Privacy is for: a formal guarantee that a mechanism's output looks nearly the same whether or not any single record was included. That's a claim about whether an observer can tell two datasets apart, not just "the numbers got noisier." The diagram below is trying to show that difference directly.

blocks.caption: At low σ, release a dozen samples and the two clusters stay apart: you can mostly tell which dataset produced which point. Drag σ up and release more. Once the clusters blur together, that loss of distinguishability is the actual privacy guarantee, not just the number moving around.

blocks.html:
In practice this means adding calibrated noise. The usual recipe is called DP-SGD, and here's the notation it uses: first pick a cap, C, the largest size any single client's update is allowed to have, and shrink ("clip") anything bigger down to exactly that size. Then pick a noise level, σ: bigger σ means more randomness added, and therefore stronger privacy. The actual noise added to each already-clipped update is a random value drawn from N(0, σ²C²), meaning a Gaussian (bell-curve) distribution centred on zero, whose spread is set by σ and C together:

noise ~ N(0, σ²C²)

In plain terms: first shrink every update so no single one can be too large or too influential (that's the clipping), then sprinkle in random noise whose size is controlled by σ. Bigger σ means more noise piled on top, which is exactly why it buys more privacy at a cost to accuracy, and there's no way around that trade-off. It's also worth being clear that SecAgg and DP aren't substitutes for each other: SecAgg hides who sent what, DP limits how much any one record could have moved the result.

blocks.label: mean RMSE at σ=2.0 versus no noise at all, measured on this thesis's own prototype

blocks.caption: Test error as the privacy noise grows, using distributed differential privacy over secure aggregation (full v6 data, 5 seeds, bars show the spread). With 36 clients the noise is averaged down and the model stays useful up to about σ = 2 (ε about 17); with 3 clients the same noise destroys it. Anything above about 0.32 is worse than ignoring the inputs. ε is my own accounting (add or remove one client, 30 rounds, δ = 1e-5), assumes secure aggregation hides each noisy contribution, and is still to be checked.

Test error after each training round on the full v6 data (untuned recipe, 5 seeds; the centralised curve is per epoch). With 36 clients, federated averaging stops improving at about 0.075, while the same clients with IID-shuffled data keep improving, so the gap comes from the differences between turbines, not from the training procedure.

blocks.html: There's mature theory for SecAgg and plenty of prior work applying FL to industrial sensor data, but nothing that puts both together on a real regression task at the client counts a wind-energy deployment would actually have. That's the gap behind RQ1 and RQ2 from the introduction, and it's time to actually answer them. A first, deliberately small prototype (one real CARE event file per farm, a small MLP, 25 FedAvg rounds) gives an early read before scaling up to the thesis's full empirical chapter:

blocks.note: RMSE in kW, the CARE dataset's normalised power units.

blocks.html:
A few things jump out. SecAgg really does cost nothing here: the FedAvg and FedAvg+SecAgg rows match to six decimal places, so aggregation privacy comes for free, and now that's shown on a regression task rather than the classification benchmarks the published SecAgg papers rely on. Keeping the data siloed at all costs more than SecAgg does: FedAvg alone is 30 to 70% worse than pooling everything centrally, which is really just the price of three physically different sites (their average temperatures alone span 20°C, 12°C and 29°C) staying separate. DP is where the real cost lives, and it's steep even at moderate noise. And small K makes dropout matter fast: with three clients and a survival threshold of two, losing one farm for a round is already close to the edge. In a 20-round dropout test, one bad round with two farms down triggered an outright abort.

Worth being upfront that this is a prototype, not the thesis's final empirical result. It trains on one ~4,000-row event file per farm rather than the full 95-file, ~19GB CARE corpus, and SecAgg's arithmetic is reproduced faithfully without an actual Diffie–Hellman exchange over a network. Its job is to sanity-check the pipeline before scaling up, which it did.

Everything above, in one place: the actual protocol visualiser built for this thesis, with federated rounds, dropout, Secure Aggregation and DP noise all running together on the real three-farm CARE topology, plus the measured RMSE curves available to overlay against its own live illustrative one.

blocks.caption: Every control unlocked at once: federated rounds, dropout, Secure Aggregation, DP noise, on the real CARE wind-farm topology.

blocks.html:
Progress note, 13 October 2026. A working update, not thesis text. The research questions below are my current framing, and my supervisor has not yet signed off their wording.

These are the two questions I am working to, in a sharper form than the proposal I started from (the introduction above still uses the original wording).

RQ1: how can secure aggregation be integrated into federated learning for cross-silo wind-turbine SCADA regression, and what does it cost in accuracy, computation and robustness to client dropout?

RQ2: what privacy-utility trade-off do secure aggregation and distributed differential privacy give, relative to centralised and local-only baselines, and how much of the gap is due to data heterogeneity rather than privacy?

Everything in this section runs on the full CARE To Compare benchmark, release v6 on Zenodo: 95 event files, 3 farms, 36 turbines. An earlier set of results used an older release of the dataset that let some test rows leak into training. I found that, reran everything on the pinned v6 release, and added checks (a file manifest, provenance stamps and a leakage test) so it cannot happen quietly again. None of the earlier numbers are used. It also means the small-sample prototype numbers earlier on this page predate the fix, so treat the numbers in this section as the current ones.

On RQ1, I have built a real, semi-honest version of the protocol, with X25519 key agreement, Shamir secret sharing so a round survives dropouts, authenticated share transport and exact integer arithmetic. It plugs into plain federated averaging, a personalised variant and distributed differential privacy. The recovered sum was bit-exact in 400 of 400 randomised trials, the masked updates look uniformly random, and training through it matches plain summation to within run-to-run noise.

The cost grows with the square of the number of clients: about 4 ms per round at 3 clients, 374 ms at 36 and 3.4 s at 100 (roughly 1,250 model parameters, one process). A round aborts when too few clients survive, and the observed abort rates match the binomial prediction: at 36 clients almost never with 10% dropout, about one round in four with 30%. The limits are real: it all runs in one process, with no signatures, no network and no active adversary.

blocks.caption: Time for one round of the real secure-aggregation protocol, with about 1,250 model parameters. It grows with the square of the number of clients because every pair of clients derives a shared secret. All parties run one after another in a single process, so this is computation only (no network), and each point is a single timing.

Chance that a round is aborted under random client dropout; a round aborts when fewer than two thirds of the clients survive. The line is the binomial prediction, open markers a simulation of the real protocol, filled markers the training runs. Only two dropout levels (10% and 30%) were run; the line in between is the formula.

blocks.label: how much worse plain federated averaging is than the centralised model at 3 clients (test error 0.0768 against 0.0236, same test data)

blocks.caption: Test error of each approach, with the ratio to the centralised model in brackets (log scale, 5 seeds, the untuned recipe used for the numbers above). Plain federated averaging is about three times worse; fine-tuning the federated model locally closes the gap. Local-only at 36 clients is held back here by its learning rate, so the tuned comparison further down is the fairer one.

blocks.html: On RQ2, secure aggregation costs no accuracy, but it only hides individual updates, not the aggregate. As a check I ran one attack: analytic gradient inversion on a single gradient, which is the best case for the attacker. On a plain update it recovers a client's row exactly; on the masked update, or on the aggregate, it does no better than guessing. Stronger attacks have not been run, and this is a semi-honest model only.

blocks.caption: How well a server can reconstruct a client's data row from an update by gradient inversion, against the number of rows behind the update (smaller error means more data recovered). A plain single-row update gives the row back to rounding error; the masked update and the sum of 36 updates are at guessing level. This is the single-gradient best case: real training (many epochs, batches of 1,024) is not inverted by this attack even without secure aggregation, so the figure shows what the protocol hides, not how likely a real leak is. One attack only.

blocks.html: A formal guarantee needs differential privacy, and that is expensive. At 36 clients the error barely moves at a small noise level and then climbs fast, and at 3 clients the same noise collapses the model, because the largest client's weight sets how much noise is needed.

blocks.note: Distributed differential privacy over secure aggregation, 30 rounds. Test error is macro RMSE in normalised power units. For scale, predicting each turbine's mean power gives about 0.32. Epsilon is my own accounting (add or remove one client, delta 1e-5), assumes secure aggregation hides each noisy contribution, and still needs checking.

blocks.html: The bigger gap, though, is data heterogeneity rather than privacy. A control where the same clients get IID-shuffled data reaches 0.0250 at 3 clients, so the pipeline is not the cause of the 3.3 times above. Personalisation closes most of it: FedPer, with personal input and output layers, reaches 0.0200 at 36 clients, level with the tuned centralised model (0.0204; 0.0236 with the untuned recipe used for the comparison above) and with local-only training (0.0207), and none of those differences are statistically significant. At 3 clients it is 7.9% worse than local-only. Fine-tuned federated averaging beats local-only by 3 to 9% at 36 clients and ties it at 3.

blocks.caption: The same comparison with every method tuned (larger network, 100 rounds, each method at its own best learning rate, 3 seeds) and with FedPer added, trained through the real protocol. Plain federated averaging stays 3.5 to 4 times worse than centralised; fine-tuning, or keeping the first and last layers on each client, closes the gap. Centralised is a reference, not a bound: per-turbine models can beat it.

blocks.html: All errors are macro-averaged RMSE in normalised power units, and the inputs include pitch and rotor speed, so they are not comparable with weather-based forecasting errors. This is one model architecture on one benchmark.

Still open: my supervisor's sign-off on the scope (a semi-honest protocol plus one attack demonstration) and on the wording of the questions; stronger attacks; and one dataset caveat, because the Farm A status labels changed between dataset releases. I treat that as a sensitivity analysis, and only plain federated averaging at 3 clients depends on it. The thesis text itself has not been started.
